paragraphs.text: For most of human history, whether other stars have planets was a question for philosophers rather than astronomers. The first planets orbiting a star like the sun were confirmed only in 1995, and since then the number known has grown to more than five thousand. It now appears that planets are the rule rather than the exception: most stars in our galaxy probably have at least one, and many have several. The discovery has transformed one of the oldest questions people have asked, whether Earth is unusual, from speculation into a subject of measurement. The pace of discovery has been so rapid that textbooks written only twenty years ago now seem out of date, and some of the planets found are only slightly larger than the moon.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Detecting such planets is extraordinarily difficult, because a planet is billions of times fainter than the star it orbits and appears, from Earth, almost in the same place. Most have therefore been found indirectly. One method measures the slight wobble of a star as an orbiting planet pulls it back and forth, which shifts the colour of its light very slightly towards blue and then towards red. This technique found the first planet around a sun-like star, a giant world orbiting so close to its star that its year lasts only four days, which surprised astronomers who had expected giant planets to lie far out, as they do in our own solar system. The shift is tiny: the motion of the star may be no faster than a person walking.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The most productive method so far watches for the tiny dip in the brightness of a star when a planet passes in front of it. A space telescope launched in 2009 monitored around 150,000 stars continuously for several years and found thousands of planets in this way. The depth of the dip reveals the size of the planet, and the time between dips gives the length of its year. Because a planet must pass directly between its star and the telescope, this method detects only a small proportion of the planets that exist, but statistics can be used to estimate how many are missed. Ground-based telescopes continue to find planets using the same method.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The planets discovered have turned out to be far more varied than those of our own solar system. Among the most common are worlds between the size of Earth and that of Neptune, a type that does not exist around the sun at all. Some planets orbit two stars at once; others are so close to their stars that their surfaces must be covered in molten rock. Such findings have forced theorists to reconsider how planetary systems form and how planets can move inwards or outwards after their birth. Some planets appear to have been thrown out of their systems altogether and drift alone through space, and some have densities so low that they have been compared to candyfloss.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Of greatest public interest are planets that might resemble Earth. Astronomers pay special attention to the habitable zone around each star, the range of distances at which a rocky planet could have liquid water on its surface. Several Earth-sized planets have been found in such zones, including some around small, cool stars that are much more common than stars like the sun. Whether these planets actually have water, or atmospheres, is another matter, since the stars they orbit often emit powerful flares that may strip atmospheres away. The nearest star to the sun has a planet of roughly the mass of Earth in its habitable zone.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The next step is to study the air of distant worlds. When a planet passes in front of its star, a little of the starlight filters through its atmosphere, and the gases present absorb particular colours. By analysing this light, astronomers have already detected water vapour, carbon dioxide and other molecules in the atmospheres of several planets, mostly large and hot ones. A space telescope launched in 2021 has greatly improved these measurements and has begun to examine smaller, rocky planets. Such measurements require observing many passages of the same planet and combining the results.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The ultimate hope is to find signs of life, gases whose presence would be difficult to explain without living organisms. Oxygen, for example, would quickly disappear from the atmosphere of the Earth if plants and microbes did not continually replace it. Researchers are cautious, however, because most such gases can also be produced by processes that involve no life at all, such as chemical reactions with rocks or light from the star. A convincing case would probably require several different gases in combination, observed repeatedly. Some claims of such gases have already been made and then disputed.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Answering the question will take decades and instruments not yet built. Plans exist for telescopes that could block the light of a star directly and photograph Earth-like planets around the nearest sun-like stars. Whatever they find, the discoveries of the past thirty years have already changed how astronomers view our place in the galaxy. The solar system, it turns out, is one arrangement among a great many, and not necessarily a typical one. Such projects will require international cooperation and many years of construction.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: For thousands of years, ships were driven across the oceans by wind. The arrival of steam in the nineteenth century and diesel engines in the twentieth ended that era, and by the mid-twentieth century commercial sailing ships had almost vanished. Today, however, the wind is returning to shipping, not as a nostalgic curiosity but as one of several technologies being used to cut the fuel consumption and emissions of the industry. Merchant shipping carries around ninety per cent of world trade by volume and produces roughly three per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, a share similar to that of a large industrial country. A few pioneering vessels have also been built to sail almost entirely by wind.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The pressure for change comes largely from regulation. The international body that governs shipping has adopted targets for reducing emissions to near zero by around the middle of the century, and some regions have begun to include shipping in their carbon pricing schemes. Shipowners must also consider their customers, a growing number of whom want to report lower emissions from the transport of their goods. Because ships remain in service for twenty-five years or more, vessels ordered now will still be operating when the targets fall due, which makes the choice of technology today particularly important. Ports are also introducing charges that favour cleaner ships.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Modern wind-assisted ships look nothing like the clippers of the nineteenth century. One design uses tall rotating cylinders, known as rotor sails, which exploit an effect first described in the 1850s: when wind blows across a spinning cylinder, it generates a force at right angles to the wind, pushing the ship forward. Another uses rigid wing sails similar to the wings of an aircraft stood on end, which can be turned automatically to catch the wind and folded down when a ship enters port or passes under bridges. A third approach attaches a large kite to the bow of a ship, flying it high above the deck where winds are stronger and steadier. The largest rotor sails are more than thirty metres tall.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: None of these systems replaces the engine. Instead, they reduce the power it must supply, typically cutting fuel consumption by between five and twenty per cent, depending on the route and the weather. Savings are greatest on routes with strong, reliable winds blowing across the direction of travel, and smallest where winds are light or come from directly ahead. Software that plans routes to take advantage of favourable winds can increase the benefit considerably, sometimes by adding only a few hours to a voyage lasting weeks. Operators report that the systems require little maintenance once installed.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Other measures offer savings of their own. Simply sailing more slowly reduces fuel use dramatically, because the resistance of water rises steeply with speed; a ship that reduces its speed by a tenth may cut fuel consumption by nearly a quarter. Coatings that keep hulls free of marine growth, which increases drag, and systems that release a layer of air bubbles beneath the hull to reduce friction are also widely used. These measures are usually cheaper than wind systems, and many shipowners adopt them first. Slow steaming, as the practice is known, became common after fuel prices rose sharply; it also lengthens voyages, which can require more ships to carry the same amount of cargo.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Such improvements cannot on their own bring emissions close to zero. For that, ships will need new fuels, and the options each have drawbacks. Ammonia and methanol produced using renewable electricity release little or no carbon when burned, but they are currently expensive and available only in small quantities, and ammonia is toxic and must be handled with great care. Hydrogen stores little energy for its volume, making it unsuitable for long voyages. Batteries are practical only for ferries and short routes. Wind assistance is attractive partly because it reduces the amount of these expensive fuels that ships will need. Some large new ships are being built with engines that can run on more than one fuel, so that owners can switch as supplies develop.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The obstacles to wider adoption are practical as well as financial. Wind systems take up deck space that might otherwise carry cargo, and they can obstruct the cranes that load and unload containers in port. Many shipowners do not pay for fuel directly, since it is often bought by the companies that charter their ships, which reduces their incentive to invest in equipment that saves it. Contracts that share the savings between owners and charterers are beginning to address this problem, but they remain uncommon. Insurers and classification societies have also had to develop new rules for ships fitted with large sails.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The return of wind to shipping is therefore a modest but significant development. It will not by itself transform the industry, but it offers savings that are available now, with technology that is already proven at sea, while the new fuels needed for deeper cuts remain scarce. In an industry where every percentage point of fuel matters, the oldest source of power at sea has once again become worth taking seriously. Shipbuilders increasingly design new vessels with space for wind systems even if they are not fitted immediately.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Should we cool the planet on purpose?

paragraphs.text: As efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions fall short of what would be needed to keep global warming within agreed limits, a once-fringe idea has moved into mainstream scientific discussion: deliberately reflecting a small fraction of sunlight back into space to cool the planet. The best-studied method, stratospheric aerosol injection, would involve releasing tiny particles high in the atmosphere, imitating the cooling that follows large volcanic eruptions. The idea alarms many scientists and environmental groups, and even its advocates describe it as a possible emergency measure rather than a solution. Its proponents insist that they are calling for research rather than use, and other methods, such as brightening clouds over the ocean, have also been proposed.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The physical principle is not in doubt. When a large volcano erupted in the Philippines in 1991, it sent millions of tonnes of sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere, where it formed a haze of particles that reflected sunlight and cooled the planet by around half a degree for more than a year. Smaller eruptions have produced similar, though weaker, effects. Laura Bennett, an atmospheric physicist, explains that a sustained programme could in principle offset a substantial part of the warming caused by greenhouse gases, and at a direct cost far lower than that of cutting emissions. She stresses, however, that this cheapness is itself a source of danger, since it would put the ability to change the global climate within reach of a single country.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Climate models suggest that the cooling would not be evenly distributed. Oren Katz, who models the climate system, points out that reflecting sunlight does not simply reverse the effects of greenhouse gases, which trap heat in a different way. Some simulations indicate that rainfall patterns, including the monsoons on which billions of people depend for their crops, could be altered, although the models disagree about how much. Katz argues that these uncertainties can be reduced by further research, but that some will remain until the method is actually tried, which is itself a risk. Regional effects are particularly hard to predict, because models differ most at small scales, and Katz also notes that the effects might differ between summer and winter.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The problem that most worries scientists is what would happen if an injection programme were stopped. Because the particles fall out of the stratosphere within a year or two, they would have to be replaced continuously for as long as greenhouse gas concentrations remained high. If the programme ended suddenly, because of war, political change or economic collapse, the warming it had masked would return within a few years, far faster than ecosystems or societies could adapt to it. This termination shock is widely regarded as the most serious physical risk of the approach. Some researchers have proposed gradual ways of ending a programme to reduce this danger.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Per Eriksson, an ecologist, warns of consequences beyond temperature. Reflecting sunlight would do nothing to reduce the carbon dioxide dissolving in the oceans, which makes seawater more acidic and threatens corals and shellfish. The particles might also affect the ozone layer and reduce the amount of direct sunlight reaching plants, with uncertain effects on crops and natural vegetation. He regards these risks as serious enough that the method should be considered only if the damage from warming becomes clearly worse than the damage the intervention might cause. Some scientists add that brighter, whiter skies would be a visible change noticed by people everywhere.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Governance may be an even greater obstacle than the science. Adwoa Mensah, a political scientist, notes that there is currently no international body with the authority to decide whether, where or how much sunlight should be reflected, and that countries would experience the effects very differently. A nation suffering from a severe heatwave might be tempted to act alone, while its neighbours bear the cost of altered rainfall. She argues that rules for research and possible deployment should be agreed before the technology is ready, rather than after a crisis has made the pressure to act overwhelming. Some countries have called for a moratorium on deployment until such rules exist.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: A related concern is that the prospect of a technical fix might weaken efforts to reduce emissions. If governments and companies came to believe that warming could be controlled cheaply by reflecting sunlight, they might feel less urgency to make difficult changes. Supporters of research reply that the opposite may be true, since the unattractive nature of the option could strengthen the case for cutting emissions quickly. Studies of public attitudes have produced evidence for both effects. The history of other environmental agreements offers some guidance but no clear answer.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The current debate is less about whether to use the technology than about whether to study it. Some scientists argue that research, including small outdoor experiments, is necessary so that decisions, if they are ever needed, can be based on evidence rather than guesswork. Others fear that research itself creates momentum towards deployment. What is broadly agreed is that reflecting sunlight could at most buy time: it cannot replace the reduction of emissions, and it would bring risks of its own that no one yet fully understands. Several planned outdoor experiments have been cancelled after public objections.
paragraphs.label: H
